chapter.name: Geographical Diversity of India
chapter.blurb: The physical geography of India: boundaries, the Himalayas, plains, desert, plateau, coasts, islands and the Northeast.

concepts.name: India's location, boundaries and five regions
concepts.description: India as the seventh-largest country, the Indian Subcontinent, its natural boundaries and the five regions used to describe it.
concepts.idea: India's mountains, desert and seas form natural boundaries that shaped its climate, culture and history.
concepts.rule: India is the seventh-largest country and part of Asia. With Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka and Myanmar it forms the Indian Subcontinent. The Himalayas lie in the north, the Thar Desert and Arabian Sea in the west, the Indian Ocean in the south and the Bay of Bengal in the east. Five regions are used: the great mountain zone, the plains of the Ganga and the Indus, the desert region, the southern peninsula and the islands.
concepts.example: The Himalayan range stands like a wall in the north of India.

concepts.name: The Himalayas: formation, ranges and importance
concepts.description: How the Himalayas were formed, their three ranges, Gaumukh and the Ganga, and why they matter.
concepts.idea: The Himalayas formed when India collided with Eurasia and are the water tower and a sacred home for millions.
concepts.rule: About 50 million years ago India, once part of Gondwana, collided with Eurasia and the land between crumpled upward. The mountains still rise about 5 mm a year. The three ranges are Himadri (Greater), Himachal (Lower) and the Shivalik Hills (Outer). Snowmelt feeds the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra, so the range is called the Water Tower of Asia. The Bhagirathi begins at Gaumukh in Uttarakhand.
concepts.example: Kath-kuni houses use local stone and wood to keep warm and resist mild earthquakes.

concepts.name: The cold desert of Ladakh and the Gangetic Plains
concepts.description: Ladakh as a cold desert with Pangong Tso and unique wildlife, and the fertile, densely populated Gangetic Plains.
concepts.idea: Ladakh is a high, dry cold desert; the plains fed by Himalayan rivers are fertile and support many people.
concepts.rule: Ladakh is a cold desert where winter temperatures fall below -30 degrees C, with little rain, rocky terrain and lakes such as Pangong Tso, a salty lake. Its landscape is called moonland. Yaks are reared for milk, meat, wool and dung and for transport. The Gangetic Plains, fed by the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra systems, have fertile soil, a large population and good road and rail networks.
concepts.example: Yaks in Ladakh give milk, meat, wool and dung and carry loads.

concepts.name: The Thar Desert and the Aravalli Hills
concepts.description: The Thar Desert's sand dunes, harsh conditions and water conservation, and the ancient Aravalli Hills.
concepts.idea: People adapt to the Thar's harsh climate, while the ancient Aravallis limit the desert's spread and hold minerals.
concepts.rule: The Thar is a vast arid region across Rajasthan, Gujarat, Punjab and Haryana with dunes up to 150 metres high, very hot days and cold nights. Rajasthan conserves water through taanka or kunds. The Aravalli Hills are about 2.5 billion years old, act as a natural barrier stopping the Thar from spreading east, and are rich in marble, granite, zinc and copper. Zawar mines show early zinc extraction.
concepts.example: Women in the desert clean utensils with sand and reuse the rinse water.

concepts.name: The Peninsular Plateau
concepts.description: The triangular plateau, the Western and Eastern Ghats, the Deccan Plateau and the rivers, forests, minerals and tribal communities.
concepts.idea: The old, mineral-rich Peninsular Plateau, bordered by the Ghats, drains through rivers flowing east and west.
concepts.rule: The Peninsular Plateau is a very old, triangular landform surrounded by water on three sides. It is bordered by the taller Western Ghats (also the Sahyadri in the north) and the lower, broken Eastern Ghats, with the Deccan Plateau between. The Godavari, Krishna, Mahanadi and Kaveri flow east; the Narmada and Tapti flow west. The plateau is rich in minerals and forests and is home to tribal communities such as the Santhal, Gond, Baiga, Bhil and Korku.
concepts.example: Rivers that flow over uneven plateau rock create waterfalls used for hydroelectric power.

concepts.name: Coasts, islands, the Sundarbans and the hills of the Northeast
concepts.description: India's 7500 km coastline, the west and east coasts, deltas, Lakshadweep, Andaman and Nicobar, the Sundarbans and the Meghalaya hills.
concepts.idea: India's varied coasts, islands, delta and northeastern hills show the variety of its geography.
concepts.rule: The coastline is over 7500 km long. The west coast runs from Gujarat to Kerala with estuaries at the Narmada and Tapti. The east coast lies between the Eastern Ghats and the Bay of Bengal with wide plains and deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri, and lakes such as Chilika and Pulicat. Lakshadweep has 36 coral islands; the Andaman and Nicobar islands are volcanic, with Barren Island the only active volcano. The Sundarbans lie in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta. The Meghalaya Plateau has heavy rainfall.
concepts.example: A delta forms when a river deposits sediments at its mouth and builds a triangular area.
